1.x: Having silenced the religious leaders in the previous chapter, Jesus now turns away from them and speaks directly to the common people and His disciples. Matthew 23 contains Christ’s final, public sermon, which consists of a blistering exposure of Pharisaic hypocrisy.

2.x: “..The scribes and the Pharisees..”: The scribes were the legal copyists and experts in the text of the Law, while the Pharisees were the prominent religious sect dedicated to enforcing strict adherence to both the written Law and their own oral tradition (which Jesus rejected). “...sit in Moses’ seat”: The “seat of Moses” (kathedra in Greek, meaning seat or chair) was a metaphorical idiom for doctrinal and judicial authority. The scribes and Pharisees were tasked with reading, interpreting, and applying the Torah to the community (metaphorically seated on Moses’ seat delivering the Law). This “judging” authority came from the Torah itself: “If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment..between plea and plea.. being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise… And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and enquire; and THEY(it was nothing like a modern Roman Pope) shall shew thee the sentence of judgment” (Deut 17:8-9 KJV). However, the scribes and Pharisees had gone beyond any legitimate authority and were adding human tradition to the Word of God (Mt 15:3-9). For that, Jesus condemned them (Mt 23:13).

The Roman Catholic Church frequently relies on Mt 23:2 to defend the papacy. They argue that just as there was an institutional, succession-based office of teaching authority in the Old Covenant (“Moses’ seat”), Christ established a parallel office in the New Covenant through the “Chair of St. Peter” (Cathedra Petri). From this, Rome derives the dogma of ex cathedra (literally “from the chair”), which is the belief that when the Pope speaks officially as the supreme pastor on matters of faith and moral, he is preserved from error by the Holy Spirit (papal infallibility). However, from an apostolic and strict biblical standpoint, the seat of Moses DOES NOT support the Catholic concept of a papacy for several reasons: (1) The Pharisaic Authority was Strictly Conditional on its Alignment to Scripture, Not Infallible: Rome claims that statements made ex cathedra are infallible and demanding of absolute spiritual obedience. However, Jesus immediately demonstrates that the authority of those sitting in Moses’ seat was highly volatile and deeply flawed. Just one chapter earlier, Jesus told the Sadducees: “YE DO ERR, not knowing the scriptures” (Mt 22:29 KJV), and in Mt 16:6, he warned his disciples to “take heed and beware of the leaven(teachings) of the Pharisees.” While Jesus tells the people to respect the civil and judicial office of the Torah reader (v.3), he simultaneously strips them of any claim to personal infallibility by spending the rest of Mt 23 calling them “fools,” “blind guides,” “hypocrites,” and “whited sepulchres.” True biblical authority is always CONDITIONAL upon a person’s alignment with the written Word of God; it is not anchored to a piece of furniture or an institutional lineage. (2) Moses’ Seat Shared Authority with Hundreds of Men Simultaneously: The Roman Catholic papacy is strictly monarchical: there is only one Pope occupying the singular Chair of Peter at any given time. Conversely, Jesus does not say a single individual sits in Moses’ seat. He says: “The SCRIBES(plural) AND the PHARISEES(plural) sit in Moses’ seat.” Moses’ seat was an office occupied by hundreds of localized judges and scholars across the ancient world simultaneously. It was not a global, centralized monarchy centered in a single city like Rome. (3) The New Covenant Expressly Rejects Hierarchical Titles: If Jesus intended to use “Moses’ seat” to set up a new system of ecclesiastical monarchies and high-ranking titles for his apostles, he completely contradicts himself just a few verses later in this exact sermon: “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven. Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ" (Mt 23:8-10, KJV) - Jesus explicitly forbids his disciples from adopting religious titles of superiority, such as “Father” (the literal meaning of the word Pope) or supreme “Master.” In the New Covenant, church leadership is structured around spiritual elders(not sacrificial priests like the Roman priests) serving as shepherds(“be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master… all ye are brethren”, Mt 23:8 KJV), with Jesus Christ remaining the sole, active head of the church. (4) Historically, the “seat of Moses” is never mentioned or commanded anywhere in the OT. It was a late, intertestamental development introduced by the rabbis during the Babylonian exile to maintain social order. By referencing it, Jesus is simply acknowledging the current civil reality of Jewish society under Roman rule, much like how he acknowledged Caesar’s currency; he is not establishing a permanent theological blueprint for the NT church.

3.x: Having acknowledged that the scribes and Pharisees occupy a legitimate civic and judicial office by reading the Torah(“Moses’ seat”), Jesus now draws a sharp line of demarcation. He warns the multitudes and his disciples that while the Scripture being read is authoritative, the behavior of the men reading it is thoroughly corrupt. “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe…”: The word “therefore” links directly back to verse 2. Insofar as these men sit in Moses’ seat and accurately read or recite the literal Law of Moses, the people are to respect and obey that Word. Jesus is not encouraging lawlessness or a rebellion against the Torah. “...but do not ye after their works..”: Do not copy their lifestyles, habits, or personal behavior. “..for they say, and do not”: They were hypocrites, reading out Scripture to the people but not living it out themselves. Their theology was vocal, but not internal. They spoke the truth with their lips but utterly denied it with their actions.

4.x: “For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne..”: The Pharisees took the pure, simple principles of the Mosaic Law and wrapped them in thousands of hyper-technical oral traditions (the halakha). They turned God’s boundaries into an exhausting, oppressive checklist of performance-based rituals that were added by men rather than God; just like how Catholicism and Orthodoxy have over-complicated the salvation process through their many Sacraments and extra-biblical requirements (such as the Councils demanding icon veneration, submission to the Pope, membership to their human organization, Mass attendance requirements, food prohibitions, placing their many mediators between their members and God, adding Sacraments to the Word of God, dogmatizing Marian doctrines, making one dependent on their priests and church hierarchy, etc). “...and lay them on men’s shoulders..”: Jesus uses the graphic imagery of a cruel master packing an immense, crushing cargo onto a beast of burden until its back breaks. “..but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers”: The Pharisees were legalistic tyrants. They strictly enforced these impossible rules on the common, working-class people, yet they used their expert knowledge of legal loopholes to exempt themselves from the real weight of those laws. They lacked any shred of pastoral empathy or mercy.

Mathew 23:5: “But all their works they do for to be seen of men..”: The core motivation behind Pharisaic religion was not the fear of God, but the craving of human applause. Their piety was entirely performative. “..they make broad their phylacteries…”: A phylactery (tefillin) is a small leather box containing parchment slips inscribed with scriptural texts (such as the Shema). Based on a literalistic interpretation of Exodus 13:9 (“And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes, that the Lord's law may be in thy mouth”, KJV) & Deut 6:8 (“And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes”, KJV), Jewish men strapped these boxes onto their foreheads and left arms during prayer. To project an image of superior holiness, the Pharisees manufactured massive, oversized boxes so no one could miss how “scriptural” they were. “..and enlarge the borders of their garments”: God commanded Israel in Num 15:38-40 to wear fringes or tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of their garments with a blue thread to remind them of His commandments. The Pharisees deliberately lengthened these tassels so they would drag and sway noticeably as they walked, loudly signaling their devotion to the crowd.

6.x: “And love the uppermost rooms at feast..”: The “uppermost rooms” refers to places of highest honor at a formal banquet table, typically the couch immediately to the right or left of the host. The Pharisees jockeyed for position, believing their religious status entitled them to social preeminence. “..and the chief seats in the synagogues”: These were the semicircular bench seats at the front of the synagogue, facing the congregation and positioned right next to the Torah scroll ark. Sitting there ensured that the entire assembly would be staring at them throughout the entire service.

7.x: “And greetings in the markets..”: They expected people to clear a path for them in public squares and salute them with deep, reverent bows. “..and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi”: They craved religious titles that elevated them above the common person, feeding their spiritual pride and cementing their control over the minds of the people.

8.x: Jesus issues a strict code of conduct for the NT church. He establishes a flat brotherhood that completely outlaws the creation of a ruling spiritual caste or the adoption of self-exalting religious titles. “But be not ye called Rabbi..”: Rabbi was an elite title meaning “my great one” or “my teacher.” Jesus commands his disciples to actively refuse this badge of social elevation. “..for one is your Master, even Christ..”: The Greek word for Master here is “kathegetes,” meaning a supreme guide or preceptor. The NKJV renders it as “Teacher” instead of “Master.” Jesus is the exclusive, definitive teacher of his church. “..and all ye are brethren”: This is a total leveling of the ecclesiastical playing field. In terms of spiritual status, value, and access to God, there is no hierarchy. Every believer stands on the same ground as a brother or sister. “Unlike the rabbis, his disciples do not make disciples of themselves or establish a succession of teachers in a chain going back to Jesus but rather bring converts into direct discipleship to Jesus. He remains the one Teacher (vv9-10), and all his followers are his disciples, who have the task of following his instructions. Baptism is part of the process of following him and accepting the position of a disciple” (Baptism In the Early Church by Everett Ferguson, pg 138).

9.x: “And call no man your father upon the earth..”: Jesus prohibits using “Father” as a formal, honorific title of religious submission or spiritual paternity. “..for one is your Father, which is in heaven”: Your existence, your spiritual life, and your ultimate accountability belong solely to God. Elevating a human being to the status of religious “Father” creates an artificial buffer between the soul and the Creator.

10.x: “Neither be ye called masters..”: Jesus repeats the prohibition using “kathegetes” again, reinforcing the absolute fidelity of the rule. Spiritual authority belong to Christ alone; no human leader has the right to demand absolute, blind submission to their personal directives.

11.x: “..the greatest among you shall be your servant”: Jesus completely redefines greatness. In the world, and in the Pharisaic system, greatness was measured by how many people served you. In the Kingdom of God, greatness is measured by how effectively and humbly you serve others.

12.x: “..whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased.. He that shall humble..shall be exalted”: This is an unalterable spiritual law. Those who climb up the ladder of religious pride and institutional titles will be violently cast down by God. Those who deliberately choose the low path of humility will be lifted up by His grace.

Catholics often defend calling the Pope and priests “Father” by pointing to passages where Paul or other NT writers refer to Abraham as a “father” (Rom 4:16: “Abraham.. Who is the father of us all”) or where Paul describes himself as a spiritual father (1 Cor 4:15). They argue that since Scripture itself uses the term “father” for men, Jesus could not have intended his command in Mt 23:9 to be taken seriously. However, this arguments overlooks the important distinctions the NT itself makes: (1) The NT recognizes spiritual fathers, but not official religious titles: Paul writes: "For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor. 4:15, KJV) - Paul calls himself a father because he brought the Corinthians to Christ through the preaching of the gospel. This is a description of a PERSONAL RELATIONSHIP, NOT AN ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICE OR HONORIFIC RULE. Nowhere does Paul instruct believers to address him as “Father Paul,” nor does he establish “Father” as an official title for church leaders. Likewise, Abraham is called “the father of us all” (Rom 4:16) because he is the historical(biological) and covenantal father of all who believe. He is not presented as the head of a continuing religious institution demanding that believers address him by an ecclesiastical title. (2) The NT rejects allegiance to human spiritual fathers: Although Paul acknowledges his spiritual fatherhood toward the Corinthians, he immediately rejects the idea that Christians should organize themselves around human leaders. The Corinthians were saying: “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I of Cephas.” Paul rebukes them: "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" (1 Cor 1:13 KJV). Again he writes: “Therefore let no man glory in men” (1 Cor 3:21 KJV). Paul understood that while God may use human servants to bring people to faith, no servant is to become the object of spiritual dependance or religious identity. Every believer ultimately belongs to Christ alone. (3) Jesus forbids the pursuit of religious titles that elevate men: In Mt 23, Jesus rebukes the scribes and Pharisees for loving positions of honor, greetings in the marketplaces, and exalted religious titles. He concludes: "But be not ye called Rabbi... And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven. Neither be ye called masters(teachers): for one is your Master, even Christ." (Matt. 23:8-10 KJV) - the context concerns official religious titles that elevate certain men above God’s people. Jesus does not deny biological fathers or the existence of spiritual mentors; rather, he forbids creating systems of religious authority that attribute to men the honor and dependence that ultimately belong to God. When Jesus gave the apostles the Great Commission, he sent them to make more disciples to him, not to them. Jesus always remains the one teacher; the disciples simply lead us to the one teacher. When people get baptized in Jesus’ name, they acknowledge their submission and discipleship to Jesus alone and to his teachings, which are brought to remembrance by the Holy Spirit (Jn 14:26), which is the divine Spirit of Christ in us: “But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV). (4) The papacy goes beyond the NT pattern: The Roman Catholic Pope is not merely recognized as someone’s spiritual father in the relational sense that Paul describes. Rather, he claims to be the UNIVERSAL spiritual father of the entire Church. Even the title “Pope” comes from the Latin “papa,” meaning “father,” and he is commonly addressed as “Holy Father.” This goes far beyond Paul’s example. Paul never claimed universal spiritual fatherhood over all Christians, nor did Peter, John, James, or any other apostle. In fact, Paul explicitly said the Gentiles were committed unto his apostleship, while the Jews were committed unto Peter’s apostleship (Gal 2:7-8). Recall that this passage comes after Paul meets with the “pillars”(plural) of the Jerusalem church: James, Peter(Cephas), and John (Gal 2:1-10). Never a single, universal spiritual leader, but different focuses for different apostleships. The NT consistently describes church leaders as “elders” (presbyteroi), “overseers” (episkopoi), shepherds(pastors), ministers, servants, or deacons - not as the universal father of the Church. Furthermore, in John 17:11 Jesus address God alone as: “Holy Father…” The NT never applies this title to any human being. (5) God alone is the universal Father of believers: The NT repeatedly teaches that all believers have one heavenly Father through Christ. Jesus said: "One is your Father, which is in heaven" (Matt. 23:9 KJV). Believers receive life through God, are adopted by God, are taught by Christ (the Father in the flesh, 2 Cor 5:19; Jn 14:8-9), and are indwelt by the Holy Spirit (God in action, Jn 4:24; 17:11). Human ministers may plant and water (1 Cor 3:6), preach the gospel, and disciple others, but God alone gives the increase and is the ultimate source of spiritual life. For this reason, Scripture allows the concept of spiritual fatherhood as a humble, relational description of one who leads another to Christ, but it never authorizes any man to claim the role of UNIVERSAL spiritual father or to receive “Father” as a permanent ecclesiastical title. Paul’s fatherhood pointed believers to Christ; it never invited them to belong to Paul. The papal claim, however, establishes a continuing office of universal spiritual paternity that the NT reserves for God alone, the one Father of all who are in Christ.

The historic adoption of the title “Pontifex Maximus” (meaning “Supreme Bridge-Builder” or “Greatest Priest”) by the papacy EXPOSES how the Roman church gradually absorbed the dress, titles, and structural styles of pagan imperial Rome. During Pagan Rome, the Pontifex Maximus was the Chief Priest of the Pagan State Religion, and was later assumed by the Roman Emperors starting with Augustus. He was the head of the College of Pontiffs, and was responsible for pagan sacrifices, ritual law, and the worshiping of dead ancestors. Late in the 4th century, Emperor Gratian (~382AC) formally rejected the title. Gratian, a Christian emperor, realized it was an inherently pagan title incompatible with his faith. During the Renaissance Era(1300-1600AC), the Popes of Rome formally adopted it into their regular official nomenclature. It was reintroduced to project imperial grandeur, appearing on papal coins, buildings, and monuments. During the early centuries, the bishops of Rome did not use this title. In fact, THEY VIGOROUSLY FOUGHT AGAINST the idea of any single bishop claiming supreme, universal titles over the global church. A prime example of this is Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great) in the late 6th century. When the Patriarch of Constantinople claimed the title of “Universal Bishop,” Gregory was absolutely outraged. He wrote letters fiercely condemning the title, calling it “proud,” “profane,” “pagan,” and a sign of the Antichrist, arguing that any bishop who attempted to elevate himself as a universal ruler over his fellow bishops was mimicking the pride of Satan. Gregory famously chose instead the humble title Servus Servorum Dei (“Servant of the servants of God”). Despite early resistance to imperial titles, as the centuries rolled on, the bishops of Rome centralized their political power. By the 15th century Renaissance, a massive cultural wave of infatuation with classical imperial Rome swept through Italy. Popes like Martin V (1417-1431) and Nicholas V (1447-1455) began officially adopting “Pontifex Maximus” and its abbreviation “P.MAX” onto their papal medals, buildings, and monuments to broadcast their supreme authority. What an early Christian emperor had cast off as pagan garbage, later Roman popes picked up and wore as a badge of honor, vividly proving that the institutional papacy had abandoned the simple, flat brotherhood commanded by Jesus in Matthew 23.

13.x: Jesus turns directly toward the religious leaders. He unleashes the first of a series of severe judicial pronouncements known as the Seven Woes. “But woe unto you..”: The word “woe” (ouai) is an expression of deep sorrow, divine grief, and impending apocalyptic judgement. Jesus is acting as the supreme judge, handing down a divine verdict upon their leadership. “..for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men..”: The Pharisees used their religious monopoly to slam the door of salvation in the face of everyday people who were searching for God. “..for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in”: They had no genuine personal relationship with God(“neither go in yourselves”), and their corrupt theological legalism actively sabotaged and blocked (“neither suffer ye” or do not permit) the sincere seekers who were trying to get to heaven, but found themselves following “blind leaders”, resulting in both falling into the ditch (Mt 15:14). God makes us responsible about who we follow; that’s why we should always be like the Bereans confirming men’s teachings with Scripture. Paul said of the Berean Jews: “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the Word with all readiness of mind, AND SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY, WHETHER THOSE THINGS WERE SO.” (Acts 17:11 KJV).

To understand HOW the scribes and Pharisees were physically SHUTTING THE DOOR TO THE KINGDOM, we need to look at the parallel account found in Luke 11:52: "Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away THE KEY OF KNOWLEDGE: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered" (KJV). In Luke’s gospel, Jesus explicitly names the instrument used to lock the door: The Key of Knowledge. In the ancient world, Torah scrolls were often kept locked in an ark or cabinet. This suggests that a Jewish scribe or lawyer who was officially ordained, would be given a physical key to the cabinet where the sacred scrolls of Scripture were locked away. This symbolized his duty to open the Scriptures and dispense their contents to the congregation. Therefore, the “Key” is the accurate declaration and explanation of the Word of God that opens up the doors of heaven to whoever possesses it.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was given an exclusive, singular set of administrative “keys” in Mt 16:19 that established him as the supreme monarch of the church. However, Jesus’ explicit wording in Mt 23:13 and Luke 11:52 completely shatters this assumption. The “Key” was the Law and the Prophets: because they sat in “Moses’ seat” (Mt 23:2), the scribes and Pharisees were the official stewards of the OT Scriptures. They were the ones responsible for preservation, copying, public reading, and preaching. The written Law was the ultimate “Key” because it pointed directly to the identity of Jesus Christ, who is the “door” to the Father (Jn 10:9). The prophecies, the sacrificial system, and the types and shadows were designed to open the eyes of the people so they could recognize their Messiah when He arrived. However, instead of using the key to open the Scriptures and guide people to Jesus, the Pharisees HID THE KEY: They buried the plain, life-giving truths of the Word under an avalanche of human traditions, oral legalism, and heavy burdens (Mt 23:4). By distorting the true meaning of the Law, they made it impossible for the average person to see Christ. When Jesus finally arrived, the religious leaders used their systemic authority to tell the public that Jesus was a demonic lawbreaker (Jn 9:24). By misinterpreting the Word, THEY LOCKED THE DOOR TO THE KINGDOM from the inside, refused to enter, and actively prevented the common people from entering the kingdom through faith in Christ. When Jesus tells Peter in Matthew 16:19: “I will give unto thee the KEYS OF THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN,” and later extends that exact same binding and loosing authority to ALL THE APOSTLES in Mt 18:18, he is not inventing a brand-new political office of a papacy. Instead, Jesus is FIRING the Pharisees and transferring the keys to his apostles. The Old Stewards (Scribes/Pharisees) abused the “Key” by hiding the true meaning of Scripture under human tradition. This resulted in the shutting up of the kingdom of heaven against men. The New Stewards (the Apostles), used the “Key” by preaching the pure, unadulterated gospel of Jesus Christ, which opened the door of faith to both Jews (Acts 2) and Gentiles (Acts 10). The very first time the apostles used this “Key” was during Peter’s first-ever preaching to the Jews in Acts 2:38: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” (KJV). By believing, repenting, and baptizing in the name of Jesus (orally invoking his name at baptism [Acts 22:16]), we submit and become his disciples and become participants in his burial and resurrection (“Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? … as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection” [Rom 6:3-5 KJV]). By following the knowledge of this “Key”, our sins are forgiven and the doors of heaven open up to us.

14.x: “..for ye devour widows’ houses…”: This is one of the most damning charges Jessu levels. Widows were the most financially vulnerable members of ancient Jewish society, fiercely protected by OT law (Ex 22:22). The Pharisees exploited their religious authority to manipulate these vulnerable women out of their assets, estates, and homes; likely through predatory financial management, unpaid legal fees, or pressuring them to donate their remaining property to the Temple. “..and for a pretence make long prayer..”: To make their cold-blooded greed, they put on a massive show of piety. They stood in public squares chanting complex, drawn-out prayers to project an aura of absolute trustworthiness. “..therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation”: Jesus reiterates the theological truth that there are degrees of punishment in hell. He had mentioned earlier how “it shall be more tolerable” for sinful cities like Sodom on the day of judgement than for cities that witnessed & rejected Jesus’ message like Chorazin & Capernaum (Mt 11:20-23). Now he states that to commit corporate theft and elder abuse under the banner of God’s name earns a higher tier of divine fury (“greater damnation”).

15.x: “..for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte..”: A “proselyte”(proselutos) was a Gentile who completely converted to Judaism, undergoing circumcision and committing to the Law. The Pharisees were highly zealous, global missionaries, traveling great distances to secure converts. “..when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves”: Zeal without truth is lethal. Because the Pharisees’ message was corrupt, their converts didn’t learn to love God; they just learned to love rules. Converts often become legalistic extremists, out-performing their teachers in fanaticism while remaining completely unregenerate. Thus, they become doubly fit for hell (“twofold more the child of hell”).

16.x: “..ye blind guides..”: Jesus changes his vocabulary here. He drops “hypocrites” momentarily to call them “blind guides.” They claim to lead the spiritual blind, yet they are utterly devoid of spiritual vision themselves. Both the “blind guide” and his followers will fall into the ditch (Mt 15:14). “..Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing..”: The Pharisees created an intricate, deceptive system of oath-making. They taught that if a man swore an oath by the physical Temple structure (or the altar, v.18; or heaven, v.22), that oath was not binding(“it is nothing”); he could break his promise without sinning. “..but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!”: However, if he swore by the gold decorating the Temple, he was legally bound(“a debtor”) to keep it and subject to the penalties of Jewish law. This arbitrary distinction betrayed their true heart: they valued financial assets (the gold) more than the dwelling place of God’s presence (the Temple). Jesus, earlier, had made it clear that swearing by those things is tantamount to swearing by God Himself, since He owns everything (Mt 5:34).

17.x: “Ye fools and blind..”: Jesus uses righteous anger to shatter their intellectual pride. In scriptural terms, a “fool”(moros) is someone who lacks moral and spiritual reality. “..for whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold?”: Jesus exposes their logical and spiritual idiocy. Gold is just a common metal dug out of the dirt; it only becomes holy(“sanctified”) because it is placed inside the Temple where the Spirit of God dwells. By elevating the value of the gold over the Temple, they had inverted reality, completely losing the concept of true holiness.

18.x: “And, Whosoever shall swear by the altar, it is nothing…”: Just as they did with the Temple building, the Pharisees taught that taking an oath by the stone sacrificial altar carried no spiritual weight. If a man swore by the altar and broke his word, they ruled that it was a non-binding promise (“it is nothing”). “...but whosoever shall swear by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty”: The “gift” refers to the animal sacrifice, grain, or fine flour offered on the altar. The phrase “he is guilty” (opheilei) is better translated as “he is bound by his oath” (BSB) or “he owes the debt.” They valued the physical sacrifice brought by the worshiper over the divine structure set apart by God. This legalistic loophole allowed dishonest men to use religious language to defraud their neighbors with systemic approval.

19.x: “Ye fools and blind..”: For the second time in this discourse, Jesus uses this severe label. He is exposing the complete collapse of their spiritual logic. “..for whether is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifieth the gift?”: Jesus brings them back to basic biblical theology. An animal carcass or a basket of grain is just ordinary, everyday agricultural property. It only becomes “holy”, set apart exclusively for God (“sanctified” split from common use), the exact moment it touches the consecrated altar. The source of holiness is the altar itself, through which God worked in the Old Covenant, not the item placed upon it.

20.x: “Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar..”: Jesus completely flattens their arbitrary, deceptive categories. He establishes that you cannot separate an object from its immediate spiritual context. If you invoke the altar in an oath, your promise automatically binds you to everything connected to the altar, including every sacrifice resting upon it, and God (v.21).

21.x: “..and by him that dwelleth therein”: The Temple is not just an architectural masterpiece or a museum of gold decorations; it is the physical location where the literal presence of YHWH God (the Father, the Holy Spirit) chose to dwell among men in the Old Covenant. When a person swears by the Temple, they are invoking the absolute authority of the Creator Himself. You cannot swear by God’s house while pretending you haven’t bound your soul to God. While the Father dwelt fully in Jesus (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19; Jn 14:9), He never stopped being an omnipresent Spirit (Jn 4:24).

22.x: “..sweareth by the throne of God..”: The Pharisees frequently swore by “heaven” as a linguistic trick to avoid using the sacred, covenantal name of God (YHWH). They thought that by leaving God’s name out of it, they could distance themselves from divine accountability. “..and by him that sitteth thereon”: Jesus completely blocks this escape route. Heaven is not empty space; it is the royal command center of the universe. To swear by heaven is to invoke the supreme majesty of the King who sits on the throne (not on a literal chair, but metaphorically speaking of God as the sovereign king over the universe and everything in it). This is why Jesus completely banned the taking of oaths altogether in the Sermon on the Mount, telling us: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mt 5:37). A true servant of God doesn't need a complex system of vows; their bare word should be as unshakeable as the throne of God.

23.x: Jesus delivers the fifth “Woe” against the religious leadership. “..for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cumin..”: The Mosaic Law commanded Israel to tithe their agricultural harvests (Lev 27:30). The Pharisees took this to an obsessive, hyper-literal extreme. They went out into their backyard gardens with tweezers, meticulously counting out one-tenth of their tiny spice leaves and seeds (mint, dill or “anise”, and cumin) to ensure perfect legal compliance. “..and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgement, mercy, and faith..”: While counting their tiny seeds, they completely dropped (“omitted”) the massive, foundational pillars of God’s character: (1) Judgement (krisis): True justice, equity, and defending the oppressed; (2) Mercy (eleos): Compassion, forgiveness, and pastoral kindness; (3) Faith (pistis): Sincere loyalty, trust, and fidelity toward God. “..these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone”: Jesus does not condemn them for tithing their herbs; he validates it as an act of obedience. However, he establishes a strict divine hierarchy: meticulous obedience to minor rituals is utterly worthless if you are living a life devoid of justice, mercy, and genuine faith.

24.x: “..strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel”: This is one of Jesus’ most famous, humorous, and culturally sharp illustrations. Both gnats and camels were classified as ceremonially unclean animals under Levitical law (Lev 11). To avoid accidentally drinking a tiny gnat that might have fallen into their wine, the Pharisees would carefully pour their beverages through a fine linen cloth or strainer. Jesus paints a comical caricature of a religious leader who is so hyper-vigilant about filtering out a microscopic bug (“strain at a gnat”), yet he unhesitatingly opens his mouth and gulps down the largest animal in Israel (“swallow a camel”). They were incredibly strict about petty details but perfectly comfortable committing massive sins like theft, pride, and corporate extortion.

25.x: “Woe unto you..for ye make clean the outside..”: Moving into the sixth Woe, Jesus uses a domestic analogy based on the strict Pharisaic rules regarding the ritual washing of household dishes (Mk 7:4). “..but within they are full of extortion and excess”: Imagine sitting down at a restaurant and being served a bowl that is sparkling clean on the outside, but caked with rotting, toxic garbage on the inside. Jesus says the Pharisees are that bowl. On the outside, their public reputation is polished and pristine. But on the inside (in their private hearts and hidden actions), they are overflowing with extortion (plundering the poor) and excess (unbridled, self-indulgent greed).

26.x: “..cleanse first that which is within..”: Jesus delivers the definitive cure for religious hypocrisy. True holiness is an inside-out process, never an outside-in performance. “..that the outside of them may be clean also”: If a person allows the Holy Spirit (YHWH’s Spirit in action) to genuinely purge their internal motives, thoughts, and desires, their external behavior will naturally reflect that transformation. You cannot fix a rotten tree by polishing its bark(protective skin); you must change the nature of the heart.

These verses stand as a perpetual warning against the spirit of legalism. True biblical holiness demands a clean interior and a clean exterior as ambassadors of Christ. However, the legalistic mind is always tempted to run to the Pharisaic extreme: (1) Imbalance of Focus: It is entirely possible to wear the right clothes, use the right religious vocabulary, and comply with every localized church tradition (“tithing the mint”), while simultaneously harboring malicious, gossiping, and unforgiving heart toward your brethren (“swallowing the camel”). Following the rules is worthless without a clean heart. The focus for salvation is always the heart, not the works, for we are not saved by works, but by the faith harbored in our hearts. (2) Performative Cleansing: God is never impressed by an external presentation that masks an unrepentant interior. If our personal prayer lives are dry, our motives are fueled by pride, and our hearts are full of hidden lust and greed, our polished outward appearance is nothing more than a clean wrapper on a spoiled product. True apostolic ministry must always place its primary premium on inward regeneration, which naturally bears the fruit of outward holiness.

27.x: Jesus delivers the final two “Woes” of this discourse. “..ye are like unto whited sepulchres..”: A “sepulchre” is a tomb. In ancient Israel, contact with a grave or a corpse made a person ceremonially unclean for seven days (Num 19:16), which would prevent them from participating in Temple worship. To prevent travelers from accidentally touching hidden graves, the Jews would paint the tombs with white lime (“whited”) every spring before the Passover, making them highly visible. “..which indeed appear beautiful outward..”: The freshly painted white tombs looked clean, bright, and even decorative against the landscape. “..but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness”: Behind the beautiful white facade lay the gruesome reality of decay: rotting flesh, dry bones, and putrefaction. Jesus says the Pharisees are walking tombs. They are highly visible, beautifully decorated, and look intensely religious on the outside, but underneath their polished behavior lies spiritual death.

28.x: “Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous..”: Jesus directly translates the metaphor. They have managed to fool human society. They wear the right robes, speak with theological precision, and perform public rituals. “..but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity”: The Greek word for “iniquity” is “anomia,” which literally means “lawlessness” or “contempt for God’s law.” Despite their obsession with the letter of the Law, their hearts are in active rebellion against the Spirit of the Law.

29.x: “..ye build the tombs of the prophets..”: Moving into the seventh and final Woe, Jesus exposes their historical delusion. The Pharisees spent vast sums of money building magnificent monuments to honor the ancient OT prophets (like Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah) who had been executed centuries earlier by the rebellious leaders of old. “..and garnish the sepulchres..”: They decorated, swept, and maintained the graves of these holy men to signal to the public how much they valued God’s true messengers.

30.x: “And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers…”: They engaged in self-righteous historical revisionism. They looked back at history and proudly claimed: “We are far more spiritual than our ancestors. We would have listened to Jeremiah! We would have protected Isaiah!”

31.x: “..ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children..”: By calling the murderers of the prophets “our fathers,” they unwittingly admitted their own genetic and spiritual lineage. Jesus is about to show them that they inherited more than just their ancestors’ DNA; they inherited their murderous hatred for the truth of God.

32.x: “Fill ye up then the measure..”: This is a chilling command of judicial abandonment. In God’s sovereign economy, there is a “cup” or “measure” of sin that a nation or group is allowed to accumulate before judgement falls (see Gen 15:16). The NIV renders this as: “complete what your ancestors started!” Jesus is telling them: “Your fathers began the work of killing God’s messengers. Now, go ahead and finish it. Top off the cup of guilt.” He knows that within just a few days, these very men will conspire to nail him to a Roman cross, and they will soon launch a bloody persecution against his apostles.

33.x: “Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers..”: Jesus closes his sermon by dropping all diplomatic language. He uses the exact same phrase that John the Baptist used to initiate his ministry (Mt 3:7). “Generation of vipers” means “brood of snakes.” By calling them serpents, he is directly linking their spiritual origin to the original Deceiver: the serpent of Genesis 3. “..how can ye escape the damnation of hell?”: This is a rhetorical question since they can no longer escape hell. They are completely blind to their own sickness, wrapped in a thick armor of self-righteous religious pride, they have rendered themselves utterly unreachable. They’ve locked themselves in an inescapable trajectory toward eternal damnation. We see this concept is 2 Thess 2:10-12: “And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.” (KJV)

The transition from dirty dishes (vv. 25-26) to whitewashed tombs (vv. 27-28) reveals a progressive depth of spiritual rot: (1) A dirty cup is merely neglected; it can be washed. (2) A tomb, however, contains nothing but permanent, irreversible death. This warns us that religious legalism is not just an annoying habit: it is a lethal, spiritual narcotic. You can dress up dead religion with beautiful church buildings, complex musical arrangements, administrative efficiency, and polished lifestyles. But if the Spirit of God is not actively regenerating the interior of the heart, we are simply sweeping the floor of a mausoleum (the little building housing a burial site). God does not want us decorated; He wants us resurrected.

34.x: Jesus transitions from a series of personal “Woes” to a cosmic, historical verdict. He is no longer speaking as a man, or just a mere rabbit, but as teh sovereign Lord (YHWH) who has sent prophets throughout history, ultimately weeping over the city that has sealed its own doom. “Wherefore, behold, I send unto you..”: The pronoun “I” here is significant. Throughout the OT, it was YHWH who sent the prophets to Israel. By stating “I send,” Jesus claims to be the same YHWH of the OT come in the flesh (1 Tim 3:16). “..prophets, and wise men, and scribes..”: Jesus is referring to the early Apostolic Church: prophets like Stephen and Agabus (Acts 11:27-28), wise men, and Spirit-led teachers who would write the NT. “..some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and some.. scourge..”: Jesus is predicting the exact fate of his disciples. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7); James was put to death with the sword (Acts 12); Peter and Paul were executed; Apostles like Peter an dJohn were scourged by the Sanhedrin (Acts 5). The Pharisees of Jesus’ day would prove they were exactly like their ancestors.

35.x: “..from the blood of righteous Abel..”: Abel was the first martyr in human history, murdered by his brother Cain out of religious jealousy (Gen 4:8). “...unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar”: he is just called “Zacharias” in Luke 11:51, but he is called “Zechariah the son of Jehoiada” in 2 Chr 24:20, where he actually gets stoned to death “in the court of the house of the LORD” (2 Chr 24:21 KJV). First, notice the “whom YE slew;” Jesus addresses the current generation as though they physically held the weapon. By walking in the same rebellious spirit, they assumed the accumulated spiritual debt of every righteous murder in history. Second, if this is Zechariah “the Son of Jehoiada,” why did Jesus call him the “son of Barachias”? There are two main solutions: (1) A Double Name / Lineage: “Jehoiada” (meaning “Yahu knows”) and “Berechiah” (meaning “Yahu blesses”) are highly synonymous spiritually. Alternatively, Berechiah may have been Zechariah’s biological father, and Jehoiada his highly famous, long-lived grandfather. Recall that “son of” in Hebrew genealogies regularly means “descendant of”. We see examples of this in Mt 1, where Matthew deliberately omits several kings in Jesus’ genealogy, showing how biblical genealogies are often abbreviated. Another example is Jesus being constantly called “son of David”, even though David lived about a thousand years earlier. Or how Joseph is called the son of Heli in Luke 3:23, but the son of Jacob in Mt 1:16, showing that “son” can refer to different family relationships depending on context. If Jehoiada was the famous priest and Barachiah was his son, then Zechariah could naturally be called both: “son of Jehoiada” (because Jehoiada raised him or was the prominent ancestor), or “son of Barachiah” (his immediate father). (2) Jehoiada may have functioned as an adoptive father: Jehoiada was already an elderly man. 2 Chronicles says he lived: “an hundred and thirty years old when he died” (2 Chr 24:15 KJV). It is possible Zechariah was born to Barachiah but raised by Jehoiada after his father’s death. The Bible sometimes identifies people by the man who raised them. For example: “Mordecai.. Brought up Hadassah..” (Esther 2:7 KJV). Although Mordecai was not her father, he functioned as one. Likewise Moses became Pharaoh’s daughter’s son (Ex 2:10). Thus one man may have both a biological father and another recognized father. (3) Jehoiada may have had two names: Many biblical people had multiple names. For example: Gideon = Jerubball (Judges 6:32); Uzziah = Azariah (2 Kings 15; 2 Chr 26); Jehoiachin = Jeconiah = Coniah; Simon = Peter = Cephas; Levi = Matthew; Saul = Paul, etc. So Jehoiada may also have been known as Barachiah. (4) Barachiah may have been a title: The name Berechiah (Barachiah) means: “YHWH has blessed.” Names in the OT often function almost like honorific titles. Examples: Melchizedek = “King of Righteousness” or Immanuel = “God with us.” So “Barachiah” could have been an honorary name rather than his legal family name. (5) Jehoiada was one of Judah’s greatest high priests, so the Chronicler would introduce Zechariah as: “Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Ch 24:20 KJV), and distinguish him by his family’s most distinguished member. (6) Scribe Transcription: A copyists’ memory may have conflated the name with the canonical prophet Zechariah (“son of Berechiah”, Zech 1:1 KJV) with what Matthew wrote: “son of Barachias” (v. 35). However, Jesus could not have been referring to the author of the book of Zechariah because he was not killed “between the temple and the altar” (v.35) like the other Zachariah did (2 Chr 24:21). Also, the phrase “from Abel unto Zechariah” is summarizing the entire Jewish OT. The Hebrew Bible begins with Genesis, where Abel dies, and it ends in 2 Chronicles, where Jehoiada’s son dies. Thus Jesus would be saying: “from the first righteous martyr in Scripture to the last righteous martyr in Scripture.” Also, Luke 11:51 omits “son of Barachias.”

Matthew 23:35 is a strong witness for the shorter Jewish/Protestant canon of Scripture as opposed to the longer Canon that Catholics have. Jesus, by saying “from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (v.35), is recognizing the Hebrew (Jewish) canon rather than the broader canon affirmed by the Catholic Church in the Council of Trent (1546). The evidence for the shorter Protestant canon is overwhelming: (1) “From Abel to Zechariah” mirrors the order of the Hebrew Bible: Today we arrange the OT as: Genesis - Malachi trying to keep a chronological order, but Jews arranged their Scriptures differently. The traditional Hebrew canon (Tanakh) is: Torah - Prophets - Writings. The last book is not Malachi but 2 Chronicles. Thus, Abel is murdered in Genesis 4 (the first book) & Zechariah son of Jehoiada is murdered in 2 Chronicles 24 (the last historical event in the last book). Jesus is therefore saying: “From the first martyr is Scripture to the last martyr in Scripture.” This is like saying today: “From Genesis to Revelation.” (2) This argument does not work with the Catholic canon: If the Deuterocanonical books are included, the last martyr in the canon is no longer Zechariah. For example: 2 Maccabees records numerous later martyrs (2 Mcc 6 & 2 Macc 7). These occur centuries after Zechariah. If Jesus were referring to the entire later Catholic canon, one might expect him to end with one of those later martyrs rather than Zechariah. Instead, he stops at the last martyr of the Hebrew arrangement. (3) Jesus repeated recognizes the threefold Hebrew canon: Luke 24:44 says: “all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalm” (KJV). This is the classic Jewish threefold division: Law - Prophets - Writings (“Psalms” representing the first and largest book of the Writings). It matches the Hebrew canon. (4) Josephus explicitly describes the shorter canon: Josephus, a first century Jewish historian, wrote around AD 90-100 in “Against Apion 1.8”: We have not an innumerable multitude of books.. But only twenty-two books…” Those twenty-two books correspond to the Hebrew canon (counted differently than today’s thirty-nine books because some books were combined, like 1 & 2 Samuel, 1 & 2 Kings, etc). Josephus also says: "No one has dared either to add anything to them, to take anything from them, or to alter anything." Yet he never includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, or 1-2 Maccabees among these sacred books. (5) Philo quotes the Greek Septuagint (LXX), but only from the Hebrew books: Philo of Alexandria (about 20BC-AD50): wrote entirely in Greek, used the LXX, frequently called it “inspired”, and quotes the OT thousands of times. Yet his quotations come exclusively from the books of the Hebrew canon. He never cites Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, or the Maccabees as Scripture. This is significant because he lived in Alexandria, the very city traditionally associated with the LXX. Although the LXX manuscripts that survive today (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) often contain the Deuterocanonical books (they contain different lists, there is no “fixed” list), Philo’s citation practice suggest that the books he treated as authoritative Scripture were those of the Hebrew canon. If Vaticanus & Sinaiticus contained extra books, it was simply because codices were used as a library of books, not as a modern “Bible” like we have today. (6) Jerome defended the Hebrew Canon: Jerome (AD 347-420), translator of the Latin Vulgate, the official Catholic Bible, repeatedly distinguished between the canonical books recognized by the Jews and the books later called “deuterocanonical.” In his Prologue to Samuel and King (“Helmeted Preface”), he wrote: “Whatever is outside these must be placed among the Apocrypha.” He then lists the books of the Hebrew canon and excludes: Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, Maccabees. He says: "The Church indeed reads Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures" (Prologue to Wisdom & Sirach). Likewise, in his preface to Judith, Jerome explains: “I have acquiesced to your request, indeed a demand, and works having been set aside from which I WAS FORCIBLY CURTAILED, I have given to this book (Judith) one short night’s work translating more sense from sense than word from word. I HAVE REMOVED THE EXTREMELY FAULTY VARIETY OF THE MANY BOOKS; only those which I was able to find in the Chaldean words with understanding intact did I express in Latin ones” (Prologue to Judith). In fact, Jerome, writing to Laeta (the wife of his friend), says: “Let he avoid all apocryphal writings, and if she is led to read such not by the truth of the doctrines which they contain but out of respect for the miracles contained in them; let her understand that they are not really written by those to whom they are ascribed, that many faulty elements have been introduced into them, and that it requires infinite direction to look for gold in the midst of dirt” (Jerome’s letter 107.12). These prefaces were part of the Latin Vulgate and were not removed until after the Council of Trent (1545), when the Clementine Vulgate was published in 1592 without Jerome’s prefaces/warnings about the apocryphal books. (7) The Glossa Ordinaria preserves Jerome’s distinction: The Glossa Ordinaria, which was the standard medieval biblical commentary used throughout Western Europe, used throughout the 12-16th centuries, and used by medieval Catholic scholars (like Thomas Aquinas), by cathedral schools, monasteries, and universities as an interpretive tool for Scripture - functioned as a common scholarly Bible commentary across Western Christendom. This official, scholarly commentary explicitly listed the Deuterocanonial books as Apocryphal, so generations of Medieval readers encountered Jerome’s statement that the books outside the Hebrew canon were not part of the canonical Scriptures. (8) Pope Gregory the Great acknowledged the distinction: In his Moralia on Job (Book 19, chapter 34), Pope Gregory the Great introduces a quotation from 1 Maccabees by saying: "We bring forward a testimony from the books, though not canonical, yet published for the edification of the Church." This shows that Gregory could regard 1 Maccabees as valuable and edifying while still distinguishing it from the canonical books. (9) Melito of Sardis: Around AD 170, Melito traveled to Palestine specifically to learn which books belonged to the Old Testament. His surviving canon corresponds closely to the Hebrew canon (with some discussion about Esther), and it does not include the Deuterocanonical books. This is one of the earliest Christian canon lists. (10) Athanasius: In his 39th Festal Letter (AD 367), Athanasius lists the books of the OT corresponding to the Hebrew canon and then distinguishes books such as Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and Esther as books appointed to be read for instruction but not placed on the same canonical level as the others. (11) Rufinus of Aquileia: Around AD 400, Rufinus, a priest in the ancient catholic church, clearly distinguished the books in the Hebrew/OT canon from other books he called “ecclesiastical” rather than canonical. In his list, he says the canon includes the books “which the fathers have comprised within the canon,” and then separately names Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees as books to be read in churches but not used to confirm doctrine. (12) Even Cardinal Cajetan defended Jerome: Just before the Reformation, Cardinal Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), the Roman Catholic theologian who opposed Martin Luther at Augsburg, wrote in his commentary on the historical books that Jerome's distinction should be followed. He treated the Deuterocanonical books as useful for edification but not as canonical in the same sense as the Hebrew books. This is significant because Cajetan died only a few years before the Council of Trent (1546), which formally defined the broader Roman Catholic canon. IN CONCLUSION, the Catholic lie that “Protestants took books of the Bibles out” is clearly a lie. In fact, the opposite is true: THEY ADDED BOOKS TO THE BIBLE.

36.x: “..All these things shall come upon this generation”: This is a direct prophecy of the catastrophic Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD. The generational “cup of iniquity” was filled to the absolute brim, and the bill for centuries of divine rebellion became due within forty years.

37.x: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem..”: The repetition of the name is a Hebrew expression of deep, agonizing grief (like “Absalom, Absalom”, or “Martha, Martha”). Jesus’ righteous anger gives way to a breaking heart. “..how often would I have gathered thy children..”: Jesus uses a tender, domestic metaphor of a mother hen shielding her chicks under her wings from a looming predator. He reveals that his ultimate desire was never destruction, but protective salvation. “...and ye would not!”: This reveals the tragedy of human free will colliding with divien love. God was willing, but the leaders of the nation chose rebellion instead.

38.x: “..your house is left unto you desolate”: The phrase “your house” is a direct reference to the Jerusalem Temple. Up to this point, God referred to the Temple as “My house” (Mt 21:13). Because they rejected the Messiah, the divine Presence departed. The Temple was no longer God’s house; it was merely “their house”: an empty, cold stone building waiting to be physically demolished by Roman legions.

39.x: “For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth..”: Jesus is withdrawing himself. This marks the end of his public teaching ministry to the nation of Israel in Matthew’s gospel. “..till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh..”: This quote is from Psalm 118:26, a Messianic greeting. Jesus is pointing to a future day of Jewish national repentance and eschatological awakening. He will not return to them as their King until they are ready to welcome Him on His terms. The Jews are not forgotten and will never be forgotten, Scripture tells of their future acceptance of the Son of God (albeit through suffering): “For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob: For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins. As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the father's sakes” (Rom 11:25-28 KJV) & "And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again" (Rom 11: 23 KJV).

Roman Catholics, Orthodox, and some historic Protestant traditions, like Presbytarians and mainline denominations, teach that the Church replaced the Jews. This is a dangerous teaching as it foments anti-semitic sentiments against the Jews, who have been historically persecuted, executed, massacred, and enslaved by the Institutionalized Empire religion (The Fourth Lateran Council, the Council that dogmatized Transubstantiation in 1215, specifically targeted the Jews, making them wear distinctive clothing and blocking them from holding political office over Christians, among other restrictions. It also led to them being falsely accused of stealing & desecrating the consecrated hosts in order to justify their abuse). The Bible teaches against this false belief: (1) Paul begins by asking the very question raised by replacement theology: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1 KJV). The answer is emphatic: “God forbid.” If Israel had been permanently replaced, Paul's answer would have been: “Yes.” Instead, he says the exact opposite. (2) "God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew” (Rom 11:2 KJV) - Israel remains “his people.” (3) Paul explains Israel’s current condition: "For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery... that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom 11:25 KJV) - notice three things: blindness is partial, blindness is temporary, and blindness lasts until. (4) Paul never says God planted a new olive tree. Instead: "And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, WERT GRAFFED IN AMONG THEM, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17 KJV) - notice how the Gentiles were wild branches, were grafted in, and share their tree. THE TREE ALREADY EXISTED. The Church did not replace the tree. It was added into it. (5) Paul explains why certain Jews are presently outside the blessings: "Because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith” (Rom 11:20 KJV) - they were not broken off because they were Jews. They were broken off because of unbelief. Likewise, Gentiles stand only by faith. (6) If replacement theology were true, this warning would make little sense: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee” (Rom 11:18 KJV) - the Church does not support Israel. Israel’s root supports the Church. Paul continues: "Be not highminded, but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 11:20-21 KJV) - the Gentiles have no reason to boast over Israel. (7) The Jews can be grafted in AGAIN. This is perhaps the clearest statement against replacement theology: "And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again” (Rom 11:23 KJV) - notice “they also,” “shall be grafted in,” “again.” You cannot be grafted in AGAIN if you have been permanently replaced. (8) The natural branches belong to the tree. Paul says: "For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature... and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?" (Rom 11:24 KJV) - notice the phrase: “their own olive tree,” not: “your olive tree,” not: “the Church’s olive tree,” but: “their own olive tree.” The natural branches are Israel. (9) Israel’s hardening is temporary. Paul again says: "Blindness in part is happened to Israel, UNTIL the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom 11:25 KJV) - the word “until” implies a change afterwards. (10) Israel will yet be saved. Paul concludes: "And so ALL ISRAEL SHALL BE SAVED: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer..." (Rom 11:26 KJV) - Paul expects a future salvation of Israel. (11) Israel is still beloved because of God’s promises. Even while many Jews reject Christ today, Paul writes: "As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sakes” (Rom 11:28 KJV) - God remembers His promises to: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, etc. (12) God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. Immediately afterward Paul says: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom 11:29 KJV) - “without repentance” means God does not revoke His gracious calling. (13) Gentiles become FELLOW HEIRS, not replacements. Paul teaches elsewhere that believing Gentiles are joined to God’s people: "That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel... But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Eph 2:12-13 KJV) - Gentiles were once strangers, aliens, far off. Now they are brought near. They were never said to have replaced Israel. Paul continues: "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints..." (Eph 2:19 KJV) - notice “fellowcitizens,” not “replacements.” (14) Gentiles become Abraham’s seed through Christ. Paul writes: “And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise” (Gal 3:29 KJV) - believing Gentiles share in Abraham’s promises through Christ. This is inheritance by union with Christ, not by replacing Israel. (15) There is one body in Christ. Paul emphasizes unity rather than replacement: "For he is our peace, WHO HATH MADE BOTH ONE… For to make in himself of twain one new man..." (Eph 2:14-16 KJV) - Christ unites believing Jews and believing Gentiles into one body. The wall is removed. The people are united. Neither group replaces the other.
